title: Bill Ackman’s $14 billion bet beyond the Magnificent 7
detail:
Bill Ackman’s $14 billion bet beyond the Magnificent 7
Opeyemi Babalola
Tue, November 17, 2026 at 4:33 PM CST 4 min read
^GSPC
META
PS
MSFT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

For three years, plenty of ordinary portfolios ran on seven engines. Anyone with an S&P 500 index fund leaned on the tech giants known as the Magnificent 7, whether they meant to or not.

That reliance got a rude reminder on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. The group lost more than $1 trillion in market value in one session, CNBC reported, on fears that the AI data center buildout could slow.

Bill Ackman had already been taking chips off that table. Pershing Square Inc. (PS), the firm he runs, sold about a third of its Microsoft (MSFT) shares in the third quarter, according to its latest 13F filing and the one before it. It also trimmed Meta Platforms (META) by roughly 11%, the filings show.

Also read: Billionaire Bill Ackman's market warning resurfaces as stocks plunge

The more telling number is what stayed.

Leaving aside its own firm and fund, Pershing held about $14 billion in stocks outside the Magnificent 7 on September 30, 2026, based on the latest filing. Those stakes make up nearly 70% of the portfolio.

Ackman trimmed Big Tech while it was rallying

The timing is the interesting part. Microsoft rallied hard in the quarter, so selling a third of the shares only shrank the position from about $2.3 billion to $2.1 billion, per the two filings. Meta's stake even grew in dollar terms.

That looks like housekeeping, not a verdict on Big Tech, and it came weeks before the November rout.

At Sept. 30 prices, the Microsoft shares sold were worth about $1.1 billion, based on the filings. Pershing's new Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) stake was worth about $1 billion, per the 13F.

Ackman effectively swapped a slice of Microsoft for the owner of the New York Stock Exchange.

ICE and Alcon are the newest names in the book

Neither appeared in the June filing, and the semiannual report of Pershing Square USA (PSUS), the firm's listed fund, says both were bought after June 30. Pershing called ICE a simple, predictable cash generator whose shares fell on worries it sees as unwarranted.

The second buy was Alcon (ALC), the Swiss maker of contact lenses and eye surgery gear. Pershing's stake was worth about $954 million at quarter-end, per the 13F.

The report argues that Alcon's roughly 20% operating margin sits well below its potential.

Netflix (NFLX) was the only existing holding Ackman added to. Pershing raised its stake by about 18% to 15.4 million shares, per the filings, even as the stock slipped.

The firm, which briefly owned Netflix in 2022, wrote that the company "has since effectively won the streaming wars."

title: Aptos lifts its APT burn rate to 2.2 million tokens a year
detail:
Aptos lifts its APT burn rate to 2.2 million tokens a year
Neo
Tue, November 17, 2026 at 1:04 PM CST 3 min read
META
Trade META on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Most blockchains create new tokens to pay the computers that keep them running. 

Aptos also destroys tokens on every transaction, and the pace of that destruction is picking up.

Aptos is a layer-1 blockchain, a base network that apps are built on, originally incubated at Meta. 

Its native token, APT, is used to pay transaction fees, and Aptos burns every one of those fees. Burning means the tokens are sent out of circulation for good.

According to the network's APT supply dashboard, last updated November 16, Aptos burned 180,626 APT in the past 30 days. 

Related: Crypto custodian BitGo puts its money on Aptos

In its end-of-October update, the network reported 170,100 APT burned over the previous 30 days.

At the current pace, Aptos projects it will burn about 2.2 million APT a year, up from the 2 million yearly pace it reported at the end of October. 

Total burns since the network's mainnet launch in October 2022 now stand at about 2.1 million APT.

Busy network, tiny fees

The burns are rising even though each transaction costs very little. Aptos says the average fee has been about $0.0005 since it raised fees tenfold earlier this year. 

Its dashboard puts the seven-day average even lower, at about $0.0003.

Those small amounts add up because of how busy the network is. Aptos processed 9.5 million transactions in a single day, according to the dashboard. In the past 30 days, users paid about $116,450 in fees, all of it burned.

Aptos says its fees are 517 times cheaper than Ethereum's and eight times cheaper than Solana's, based on seven-day averages.

A smaller gap between new and burned APT

New APT still enters circulation faster than it is removed. Aptos pays stakers, the users who lock up APT to help secure the network, an annual reward rate of 2.6%. That creates about 1.6 million new APT a month. 

After burns, net new supply comes to about 1.4 million APT a month, the dashboard shows.

That gap was much wider before this year. In March, APT holders voted to cut staking rewards from 5.19% and to cap the token's total supply at 2.1 billion. Aptos supply currently sits at about 1.2 billion APT.

Aptos says every burn can be checked on the blockchain itself. As activity grows, each month's burns cover a larger share of the new APT the network creates.

An $11 Billion Fund Dumps These 2 Stocks ©Kittipong Jirasukhanont from PhonlamaiPhoto's Images, Nikada from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Key Takeaways

Atreides Management, an $11 billion fund, sold all of its Amphenol and Alphabet shares in the third quarter and more than doubled its stakes in Astera Labs and Meta Platforms.

The Alphabet exit isn't a clean one, since the fund held Alphabet call options with $688 million of notional value at Sept. 30.

Analysts see more than 40% upside in both stocks the fund sold, and Amphenol's average price target is at its high for the year after a record quarter.

Of the two stocks the fund sold, Amphenol looks like the better buy today.

Atreides Management sold every share it held of Amphenol (APH:NYSE) and Alphabet (GOOGL:NASDAQ) in the third quarter. That's from its 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 16. The firm manages $10.7 billion, and neither stock is among its 41 positions now.

In the same quarter, it more than doubled its stakes in Astera Labs (ALAB:NASDAQ) and Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ), which are now its No. 2 and No. 3 positions. But the Alphabet sale isn't what it looks like.

Atreides still has a big Alphabet bet

At June 30, Atreides held 488,296 Alphabet shares worth $175 million, or 1.6% of its 13F stocks. By Sept. 30, the shares were gone. But the same filing shows call options on Alphabet with $688 million of notional value, nearly four times what the shares were worth at June 30.

A 13F doesn't say when a fund traded, what it paid or why. Still, it's hard to call this a vote against Alphabet. The fund sold its shares and still had a lot riding on the stock at Sept. 30.

Analysts still see big upside in Alphabet

Alphabet is 31% below its 52-week high, and Wall Street hasn't given up on it. The 58 analysts who cover it have an average price target of $400, 41% above the last close. That average has climbed over the past year, though it has come down from its peak:

Alphabet (GOOGL): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

The average target was $317 a year ago and peaked at $433 in late July. Over the same year the stock has barely moved: it closed at $284, against $285 a year ago. It trades at about 21x forward earnings.

TIKR tracks 19 analysts on Amphenol. How many say "Buy"?

Amphenol posted a record quarter after the fund sold

Amphenol was the cleaner exit. At June 30, Atreides held 640,069 shares worth $113 million, or 1.0% of its 13F stocks, and the Sept. 30 filing shows no shares and no options.

Renaissance Technologies slashed its Nvidia stake 99.7% in one quarter, and Micron and AMD replaced the chipmaker as its largest holdings.

Renaissance also gutted Meta, Apple, Amazon and Broadcom by more than 99%, signaling a broad rotation out of mega-cap tech.

Nvidia's revenue more than doubled while Renaissance sold, so the stale quarter-end filing says less than the company's own execution.

Renaissance Technologies, the quantitative hedge fund started by the late Jim Simons, cut its stake in NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) from 7,091,256 shares on June 30 to just 23,170 shares on Sept. 30. That is a 99.7% reduction, disclosed in a 13F filed Nov. 12. On June 30, the position was worth $1.42 billion, making it the largest reported holding for the fund on that date. It placed ahead of a Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) stake valued at $1,139,611,745.

gleuschk / Flickr

Even at a high-turnover shop like Renaissance, the near-total exit from a top holding in one quarter stands out. By Sept. 30, Micron Technology (NASDAQ:MU) had become the fund's largest position at $1,619,650,963. Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) was second at $1,205,536,416.

Five Mega-Cap Tech Stakes Nearly Vanished in One Quarter

Renaissance cut several other tech giants just as hard that quarter. Meta fell 99.9% to 1,577 shares. Apple fell 99.8% to 3,246 shares, and Amazon fell 99.5% to 11,128 shares. Broadcom fell 99.9% to 734 shares. The fund also took a fresh 4,113,200-share stake in SpaceX. Taken together, the moves show a sharp reduction in several mega-cap tech positions, although Renaissance increased holdings in other technology companies, including Micron and AMD.

title: Prediction: These 2 Stocks Will Be Worth More Than SpaceX 5 Years From Now
detail:
Prediction: These 2 Stocks Will Be Worth More Than SpaceX 5 Years From Now
Rick Orford, The Motley Fool

SPCX
AVGO
NVDA
META
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

SpaceX (NASDAQ: SPCX) has become one of the biggest names on Wall Street since its June debut, and currently has a market cap of almost $19 trillion, but two other tech giants could be worth more within the next five years. Specifically, Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO) and Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) are both well-positioned to benefit from the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, potentially pushing both companies' market caps past SpaceX's by 2031.

Image source: Getty Images.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Broadcom could be one of the biggest winners in the AI boom

The world's largest tech companies are increasingly designing custom AI chips and networks tailored to their own computing needs, and Broadcom has become a key partner in that effort. The results are already showing up in the numbers.

In fact, Broadcom reported strong growth in its AI semiconductor business, driven by steadily rising demand for custom AI accelerators and networking technology. In its fiscal third quarter, AI semiconductor revenue grew 221% year over year to $16.7 billion. Management also indicated that momentum continued into the current quarter as the AI build-out accelerated.

Broadcom's expanding position selling the picks and shovels to multiple companies in the AI race could potentially make it more valuable than SpaceX in the next few years.

Looking ahead, if hyperscalers and AI labs continue shifting more of their workloads to custom chips, Broadcom will benefit from industrywide spending. That could be a more sustainable model than relying on the success of any specific consumer-facing platform.

Still, Broadcom faces a number of risks. In particular, any slowdown in AI infrastructure spending by its largest customers could impact its revenue growth. There are also concerns about its high degree of customer concentration and whether investments in AI will ever generate attractive returns.

Meta uses AI to turn its massive ecosystem into a growth engine

The case for owning Meta has changed considerably over the past year. Instead of its AI-related spending being viewed as an expensive long-term investment, AI has become a part of the company's core business. And it's turning into a major advantage.

Meta already has billions of people regularly using Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Messenger, along with millions of businesses spending money on its advertising platforms. As a result, Meta can deploy AI directly across that massive ecosystem.
